newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen up at open, Dow eyes 8,000.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen up at open, Dow eyes 8,000.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open higher Wednesday, with the Dow industrials powering past the 8,000 level soon after the opening bell, analysts said.

A psychological desire to hit 8,000, upbeat prospects for second quarter earnings, an absence of threatening economic data, and strong earnings at technology giant Motorola Inc will propel share prices upward, they said.

"I think we are set for a higher open," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities. "There is nothing to intervene and we are 38 points away from the big round number, the mother of all round numbers."
In early trade the Standard & Poor's 500 futures index was up 0.95 point at 928.75, while the long bond was up 5/32 at a yield of 6.57 percent.
On Tuesday the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at a record high 7962.31, up 103.82 points. The Nasdaq composite index finished up 14.36 points at an all-time high 1485.10.
Analysts said the market could see profit-taking if the Dow tops 8,000.

Motorola's strong quarter could boost share prices, but weaker-than-expected quarterly results from chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices Inc could spook technology stocks, said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
"Motorola's numbers were really good, but then we had a disappointment from Advanced Micro, so it might be sort of a wash," Cardillo said.
In London trading, shares of Motorola rose, while Advanced Micro slipped, as did shares of rival chipmaker Intel Corp .
"We will probably go above 8,000 but we will not necessarily close above that," Cardillo said.
Wachtel said the stock market might take Advanced Micro's results in stride, having expected the second quarter to be a transition period for the company.
Motorola posted second quarter earnings of $0.62 per share, excluding a charge, compared to a First Call estimate of $0.56 and the year-earlier $0.54.
Advanced Micro reported earnings of $0.07 per diluted share compared to a First Call estimate of $0.22.
Tobacco stocks might also ease slightly, following newspaper reports that the White House may reject a key element of the proposed $368 billion tobacco settlement, Cardillo said.
Japan's Nikkei average closed off 156.72 points, or 0.79 percent, at 19,697.17.
In London, the FTSE 100 was up 13.2 points at 4771.7. U.S. stocks were mixed in light trade in London.
The dollar clawed back from earlier lows against the yen, due to short covering. In Tokyo the dollar was trading at 112.77/79, while in Europe it was trading at 1.7606/16 marks.

The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that investors who can deal with the possibility of lower gold prices could see the benefits of the expected consolidation in the industry, according to analysts.

The New York Times said in its Market Place column that Dutch financial firm ING Groep N.V., which agreed to buy Equitable of Iowa Cos for $2.2 billion, is ready to spend more money to meet ambitions in U.S. markets. ((--Wall
Street Desk 212-859-1730))
